strengths: Addresses a clear limitation of prior NeRF-weight processing methods: dependence on a fixed NeRF architecture. The idea of using Graph Meta-Networks over parameter graphs is well motivated and relevant.
The paper is clearly written, with a coherent method description and useful separation of rendering-only, contrastive-only, and combined objectives.
Experiments cover both classification and retrieval, and the latent-space analyses help explain why the different losses behave differently.
The unseen-architecture experiments are a valuable step beyond standard same-distribution evaluation, showing some ability to process architectural variants without retraining.
weaknesses: The central claim of handling arbitrary or unseen NeRF architectures is substantially overclaimed. Training uses only MLP and tri-plane NeRFs, while unseen architectures are mostly minor hyperparameter variants within the same families. No hash-grid, voxel-grid, Gaussian/modern radiance-field, or practitioner-standard architectures are evaluated.

Novelty is moderate: the method is largely a combination of existing GMN parameter-graph machinery, the nf2vec decoder/rendering loss, and a standard SigLIP-style contrastive loss. The paper would benefit from a sharper technical contribution beyond assembling these components.

The empirical evidence is limited to synthetic ShapeNet object-centric NeRFs and two prior datasets. This leaves unclear whether the method scales to real scenes, larger fields, view-dependent effects, higher-resolution encodings, or state-of-the-art NeRF variants.

Baselines are weak in the multi-architecture setting: prior methods are marked inapplicable, but the paper does not explore simple adaptation baselines, separate encoders with shared embedding alignment, architecture-specific encoders plus contrastive training, rendered-view baselines, or parameter-statistic baselines.

Some results weaken the main narrative. Instance-level retrieval remains modest, with recall@1 around 44-45% in cross-architecture settings and 29% for BOTH/BOTH under the best model; LR completely fails for instance retrieval. Several unseen tri-plane variants, especially TRI-8C and TRI-16W, show large drops, suggesting limited robustness.

There is little analysis of scalability and computational practicality. Training takes around two weeks for LR/LR+C on a single RTX 3090, but runtime, graph sizes, memory costs, and feasibility for larger NeRFs are not characterized.

Ablations are incomplete: there is no sensitivity analysis for the contrastive weight, batch size, graph features, encoder depth, embedding size, decoder capacity, or alternative contrastive objectives.

Reproducibility details are partial. The paper describes architectures and hyperparameters, but does not clearly state whether code, trained models, graph-conversion routines, and all generated unseen-architecture datasets will be released.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: directly processing NeRF weights when the underlying NeRF architectures differ, which is a real limitation of prior weight-space NeRF processing methods.

The core idea of using Graph Meta-Networks to encode parameter graphs of different NeRF architectures is natural and technically plausible, and the combination with a contrastive objective is well motivated.

The paper provides a reasonably clear experimental story across classification, class-level retrieval, instance-level retrieval, and unseen architecture variants, showing that the contrastive loss improves cross-architecture alignment.
The results are internally consistent: rendering loss improves class separability, contrastive loss improves architecture invariance, and the combined loss often trades off between the two.
The appendices include useful implementation details, model hyperparameters, dataset descriptions, and compute information.
weaknesses: The main claim of handling arbitrary NeRF architectures is substantially overstated. The experiments cover only MLP NeRFs and tri-plane NeRFs, plus small variants of those architectures. Important practical NeRF families such as hash-grid or voxel-grid based methods are not evaluated.

The “unseen architecture” evaluation is weak. Most unseen settings are minor changes to hidden dimension, layer count, tri-plane width, or channel count, rather than genuinely different architectural families. This does not convincingly establish architecture-agnostic generalization.

The baselines are limited. The paper mostly compares against nf2vec and Cardace et al., which cannot operate in the multi-architecture setting, leaving many tables without real competing methods. Stronger baselines such as separate encoders with shared embedding alignment, rendered-view baselines, direct supervised GMN training, or other weight-space/meta-network approaches are missing.

The evaluation is narrow: all experiments are on synthetic ShapeNetRender object-centric NeRFs with simplified radiance fields and no viewing direction. This limits the significance for realistic NeRF usage, scenes, and modern neural field pipelines.

The retrieval results are mixed. Instance-level retrieval remains far from solved, with recall@1 around 44-46% in the cross-architecture setting and 29% for BOTH/BOTH even for the best variant, yet the paper presents the framework rather positively.

The method is computationally expensive: training LR or LR+C takes about two weeks on a single RTX 3090. The paper does not adequately analyze scalability with graph size, number of parameters, or more complex NeRF architectures, which is critical for the claimed generality.

The technical novelty is moderate. The paper combines existing GMNs, nf2vec-style rendering loss, and SigLIP-style contrastive learning; the contribution is mainly an application and empirical study rather than a fundamentally new method.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence supports, especially statements such as “handle any input neural architecture” and “arbitrary NeRF architectures.” The actual demonstrated scope is much narrower.

Ablations are incomplete. The paper does not sufficiently isolate whether gains come from contrastive alignment specifically versus additional supervision, batch construction, embedding normalization, or simpler domain-alignment losses.

The paper would be stronger with deeper analysis of failure cases, robustness to NeRF training quality, object identity leakage across paired datasets, sensitivity to lambda and batch size, and performance on downstream tasks beyond classification/retrieval.

strengths: Clear and timely problem: learning directly from NeRF weights across heterogeneous NeRF architectures is a meaningful limitation of prior weight-processing methods such as nf2vec and tri-plane-specific approaches.
The proposed combination of parameter-graph conversion, a Graph Meta-Network encoder, the nf2vec-style decoder, and a contrastive SigLIP-style objective is technically sensible and well motivated.

The paper provides useful empirical evidence that rendering loss alone clusters embeddings by architecture, while the contrastive objective improves architecture-invariant organization, classification transfer, and cross-architecture retrieval.
Experiments cover both multi-architecture and single-architecture settings, include comparisons to relevant prior methods where applicable, and add tests on several unseen architecture variants.
The presentation is generally clear, with good qualitative latent-space and retrieval visualizations and sufficient architectural/training details in the appendix.
weaknesses: The central claim of handling arbitrary NeRF architectures is stronger than the evidence: experiments are limited to MLP NeRFs and tri-plane variants, with unseen architectures mostly being modest hyperparameter changes rather than genuinely different modern NeRF families such as hash-grid or voxel-grid methods.

The multi-architecture setting lacks direct external baselines, so the strongest empirical claims are mostly supported by ablations among the authors' own variants rather than comparisons to adapted alternatives.
The practical impact is somewhat limited because the evaluated NeRF architectures are not state-of-the-art, and the authors themselves note that commonly used hash-table architectures are not tested.

Instance-level retrieval remains far from solved, especially in the BOTH/BOTH case, where even the best recall@1 is 29.0%, suggesting the learned representation is useful but not yet robust for fine-grained cross-architecture matching.

Computational cost and scalability are concerns: training takes days to weeks on a single RTX 3090, but the paper gives limited analysis of graph sizes, memory/runtime scaling, or feasibility for larger and more complex NeRFs.
Reproducibility would be stronger with clearer discussion of code/data release, variance across runs, and sensitivity to the contrastive weighting and batch construction.

strengths: Addresses a timely and well-motivated problem: learning directly from NeRF weights when the underlying NeRF architectures differ. This is a real limitation of prior weight-space NeRF processing methods such as nf2vec and tri-plane-specific approaches.

The method is technically coherent: using Graph Meta-Networks as an architecture-flexible encoder is a natural but effective choice, and the contrastive SigLIP-style objective directly targets architecture-invariant embeddings.

The paper makes a concrete extension by proposing a parameter-graph construction for multi-resolution hash-table NeRFs, enabling weight-space processing of a widely used NeRF family not covered by prior work.

Experiments cover multiple architecture families and several held-out architectural variants, showing that the approach can generalize within seen families and that the contrastive term improves cross-architecture transfer and retrieval.

The ablations over rendering loss, contrastive loss, and their combination are useful and support the main design choice. The latent-space analysis, classification tables, and retrieval results tell a mostly consistent story.
Writing and positioning are generally clear, with enough implementation detail in the appendix to understand the model, graph construction, losses, and training setup.
weaknesses: The evaluation is still narrow relative to the strength of the claims: almost all quantitative experiments are on ShapeNetRender object-centric NeRFs, with only qualitative Objaverse retrieval. There is no strong evidence for robustness on real scenes, diverse capture conditions, larger-scale datasets, or full NeRF formulations with view direction.

The method only demonstrates generalization to architectural variants within families seen during training. It does not show transfer to genuinely new architectural families, despite the framing around arbitrary or diverse NeRF architectures.

Baselines are somewhat limited. Prior methods cannot handle the multi-architecture setting, but the paper could include stronger practical alternatives such as rendering-based multi-view classifiers/retrievers, architecture-specific adapters, simple statistics over weights, or separate per-architecture encoders with alignment.

The retrieval results, one of the more architecture-invariance-focused evaluations, are modest in absolute terms: for ALL/ALL, LR+C reaches only 5.3 Recall@1 and 27.2 Recall@10. The paper presents qualitative retrievals, but the low quantitative performance weakens the claim that instance-level architecture-agnostic representations are strong.

Some reported results are mixed: LR often outperforms LR+C when the classifier is trained on all architectures, and several unseen variants show severe degradation, especially TRI-8C and HASH-11T. This suggests the learned representation is not uniformly architecture-agnostic or robust to seemingly modest design changes.

The hash-table graph construction is memory-efficient, but it appears to discard much of the spatial/hash topology and interpolation structure. The paper does not deeply analyze whether this representation is theoretically justified or compare it to alternative graph encodings beyond arguing scalability.

The computational cost is high, with training taking about two weeks on an RTX A6000 for LR or LR+C, and reproducibility may be challenging without released code, trained NeRF datasets, and pretrained checkpoints. The paper mentions implementation sources but does not clearly state artifact availability.

The significance is promising but not yet fully established: the downstream tasks are limited to classification and retrieval, and the work does not show impact on broader NeRF workflows such as editing, compression, quality prediction, retrieval at web scale, scene understanding, or NeRF-language tasks.

strengths: The paper targets a meaningful limitation of prior NeRF-weight processing methods: dependence on a fixed NeRF architecture. Handling MLP, tri-plane, and hash-table NeRFs within one encoder is a relevant problem for neural field representations.

The proposed use of a Graph Meta-Network is technically plausible, and the paper gives a concrete parameter-graph construction for multi-resolution hash tables. This is a useful engineering contribution, even if conceptually modest.

The experiments cover 13 architecture variants and include both classification and retrieval settings. The results show that the contrastive term improves cross-architecture transfer compared with a rendering-only loss, especially when the classifier is trained on one architecture and tested on another.
The manuscript is mostly clear and includes implementation details such as model sizes, optimizer settings, training time, and dataset splits.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. The main method is largely a combination of an existing GMN encoder, the nf2vec decoder/rendering loss, and a standard SigLIP-style contrastive objective. The hash-table graph conversion is the most original component, but it is not deeply analyzed or compared against alternative graph encodings.

The multi-architecture comparisons are weak because the main baselines are simply declared inapplicable in many tables. A stronger paper would adapt or ensemble single-architecture baselines, compare against rendered-view classifiers/retrievers, compare against direct feature statistics or architecture-specific encoders, and quantify the cost/performance tradeoff.

The retrieval results are not very convincing. Instance-level Recall@1 is only 5.3% for ALL/ALL and remains low for several cross-architecture settings, so the claim of an architecture-agnostic instance-level latent space is only partially supported.

The evaluation is narrow despite the number of architecture variants. Nearly all quantitative experiments use ShapeNetRender, with Objaverse used only qualitatively. This leaves open whether the approach generalizes across datasets, object distributions, real scenes, or more realistic NeRF formulations with view-dependent effects.

Some reported results undercut the central story: the rendering-only objective is often better for classification when training and testing are aligned, while LR+C trades off class separability for architecture invariance. The paper does not sufficiently characterize when this tradeoff is desirable or how to choose the objective in practice.

The unseen-architecture experiments are limited to variations within known families and often show sharp failures, such as low performance on changed tri-plane width/channels or hash-table size. This weakens the broader framing of architecture-agnostic inference.

There is little statistical analysis: no confidence intervals, repeated runs, significance testing, or robustness analysis, despite long training times and potentially high variance in representation learning.

The practical significance is unclear. Training takes about two weeks per LR/LR+C model on an RTX A6000, but the paper does not analyze inference efficiency, memory usage, graph size scaling in practice, or whether avoiding rendering is actually advantageous relative to strong rendered-view pipelines.

The paper's claims are somewhat stronger than the evidence supports, particularly around being generally architecture-agnostic and suitable as a foundation for NeRF weight processing. The demonstrated contribution is narrower: limited cross-architecture representation learning on object-centric synthetic NeRFs.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear and timely limitation in neural-field weight processing: prior NeRF-weight methods are tied to fixed architectures, while this work studies embeddings across MLP, tri-plane, and hash-grid NeRFs.

The technical approach is sensible and well-motivated, combining Graph Meta-Network parameter-graph encodings with the nf2vec-style decoder and a contrastive SigLIP objective to encourage architecture-agnostic embeddings.

The experimental study is broader than prior NeRF-weight-processing work, covering 13 architecture variants across three families, including hash-table NeRFs, and evaluating both seen and unseen architectural hyperparameter variants.

The ablation between rendering-only, contrastive-only, and combined objectives is informative: the paper shows a meaningful tradeoff between class separability and architecture invariance, and the combined loss is clearly beneficial for cross-architecture retrieval and transfer.

Results are strong for classification in many settings, including competitive or better single-architecture performance against nf2vec and Cardace et al., and substantial gains when training and test architectures differ.
The paper is clearly written, with useful diagrams, detailed appendices, and enough architectural/training details to understand the method and reproduce much of the setup.
weaknesses: The novelty is incremental in components: the main method largely combines existing GMNs, nf2vec decoding, and contrastive learning. The new hash-table parameter graph and cross-architecture NeRF study are valuable, but the algorithmic contribution is not especially deep.

The claim of architecture-agnostic or arbitrary-architecture processing is overstated. The method requires hand-designed graph conversions and is only tested on variants within seen architecture families; there is no evaluation on a truly unseen NeRF family such as voxel grids, tensor decompositions, Gaussian-like neural representations, or modern scene-level variants.
The evaluation is heavily centered on ShapeNetRender synthetic object-centric NeRFs. The Objaverse experiment is only qualitative, so evidence for dataset-level generalization is limited.

The multi-architecture comparisons are somewhat constrained because prior methods are marked inapplicable rather than adapted into reasonable baselines. Additional baselines such as render-and-classify, per-architecture encoders with shared embedding alignment, simple weight statistics, supervised contrastive variants, or architecture-ID-conditioned models would make the evidence stronger.

Retrieval results, while much improved by the contrastive term, remain modest in absolute terms for several cross-architecture pairs, especially involving HASH/TRI and HASH/MLP. This weakens the claim that the learned space reliably captures instance-level identity across architectures.

Some classification results reveal brittle generalization to certain architecture changes, e.g. TRI-8C and HASH-11T, but the paper mostly reports these as observations rather than analyzing failure modes or proposing remedies.

The paper does not report variance across random seeds or confidence intervals, which matters given the expensive training, many tables, and several close or inconsistent comparisons between LR and LR+C.

Reproducibility is only partial: implementation sources are described, but there is no clear statement about code/model/dataset release. The reported training cost is high, about two weeks on an RTX A6000 for LR or LR+C, which may make independent replication difficult.
